speaker: Ben Stokes
quote_text: Ben, I’ll just start by saying thank you. I  think I speak for most of us, if not all of us, by saying you’ve really engaged with this and  you’ve given us plenty of your time, and there are places you’d rather be, I’m sure, and people you’d  rather be with. So thanks for that. First of all, I guess you’ve had a lot of time to reflect on  this over the last 24 hours, and you’ve done a bit of chatting around the place. What would you like  to think now that your legacy with this team is, with your teammates or the fans? God. Well,  first of all, I’d say the feel in this room is a lot different to what it was six or seven  days ago. I’ll give that one. But I don’t know, really. Again, you could ask all the supporters  of English cricket that same question and you’ll probably get a few different answers. And, you  know, I guess everyone’s got the right to say what they want and whatever. But I guess for  me, I’ll just say that I feel like I’ve given as much as I could have done to England over the  years that I’ve been lucky enough to represent this team. And I guess that’s the one thing  that I hope everyone will be able to say, is that he left everything out there at every single  opportunity that he got to wear the shirt. Because there’s certainly something that I always sort of  told myself to make sure I do is, regardless of what goes on in terms of the returns, whether it  be with the bowling or batting, just as long as you’re going out there and making sure that you’re  giving absolutely everything every single time, then you can hold your head high. So from that  account, I feel like I can hold my head pretty high. And there’s been a lot of talk so far about  your future, what your next move is, what you do next, when we may or may not see you again. I  wonder about the future of the team. How do you reflect on where you’re leaving this team versus  where you picked it up? Yeah, well, I announced I was retiring yesterday and then I’ve had a few  questions asking if I’m going to be able to sit on my sofa watching next year. I mean, I know it’s  the Ashes next year, but I’ll probably be watching it in a hospitality box somewhere, not thinking  about what’s going on in the field. But look, I think this team has all the capabilities in the  world to be able to go on and achieve what I think it should be able to achieve. And look, I’m one  individual in a sport that requires 11 people to go there and achieve what every team wants  to achieve, which is to win. And, you know, there’s a lot of time to go before, obviously,  the big bull, which is the Ashes in 2027, for things to be able to take place. But the  people who are in that dressing room now, I’ve got absolute confidence they’ll be able to go  on and do what needs to be done in terms of taking the team forward. You know, I feel like I’ve,  as I’ve just said, given everything to the team as a player, and I can be happy that I’ve given  everything I could to the team as a captain over four and a half years. In a comical way, I guess  I can say, not my problem anymore. But yeah, look, I’ll still be following this team with as much  interest as ever. I love the England cricket team. I’ve got a serious passion for seeing the  team do well and that’s not going to change just because I’m not in the dressing room anymore.  And you’ve been a big personality in this job, you know, out there on the field, in the dressing  room, even talking to us, putting messaging out there. Do you think that there are people there,  leaders who can step up and fill what is a pretty big gap now? Yeah, definitely. And look, you go  back to when I got asked to do it, I think there were a lot of people saying, no, I’ve got  no experience in captaining or leadership. It’s too much for me to take on my shoulders  because of the role that I play in the team. I was being compared to the other great all-rounders  that were before me because of how things went for them. But there are leaders in that group  who, whoever is asked to take the team forward, they’ll be able to put their own stamp on this  team because that’s what I’ve tried to do. And it shouldn’t be any different for whoever  gets the honour of taking this team forward from the series against Pakistan. Do you feel  Harry Brook is ready to take that baton from you, your vice-captain? Yes, I do. There’s a reason  why he was asked to be vice-captain of this team. I know that, again, with all the controversy  over the last couple of weeks, there were some decisions that were made, but those were  decisions that I wasn’t part of making. You know, you’re asked to be vice-captain of a team for a  certain reason. I was vice-captain under Joe for a long time. And it’s a natural progression. The  captain’s not there or unavailable, then you step up to be that. So there’s absolutely no reason  why Harry shouldn’t be asked to do that. You know, he’s someone who is obviously an incredible  player, one of the more senior players in this group. And look, we all know he’s a phenomenally  talented individual when it comes to his skill as a batter. And if you lump a bit more  responsibility on the shoulders with this team, we don’t know if that’s going to show any more  improvement in the skills that he’s already got. Only time will tell. But you don’t ask someone to  be vice-captain if you don’t think that they’ve got the skills and the ability to be able  to captain the team when they need to. So if I was to be asked who I think should do it, I’m  throwing my 100% support behind Harry Brook. And do you still believe that Brendon McCullum and Rob  Key are the right people to take the team forward? What me, Brendon and Rob have managed to do over  four and a half years has been, not going to lie, quite an interesting ride if you take it for what  it is. We’ve had some incredible highs, we’ve had some pretty low lows as well, but I feel it’s  always worked and connected pretty well in terms of what we want to achieve. And we’ve always had  that direction of how do we get the team better, how do we take them forward? And it doesn’t always  work out the way that you want it to work out. Again, I’m done now. I don’t have to make those  decisions. I don’t have to be involved in all that kind of stuff. And I’m being honest, one of the  nice feelings about being in the situation that I find myself in now is that I don’t have to worry  about that stuff. But I’ve thoroughly enjoyed my four and a half years working relationship with  Brendon and Rob. And then there’s other decisions to be made that we have to give a shit about now.  I was going to ask about Rob and Brendon as well, so said one, Harry. You think you would  choose Harry to be the next captain, his relationship with Brendon. Do you think  those two as a combination can take the team forward into next year’s Ashes? Yeah, I think so.  I think the most important thing with whatever happens going forward is that there needs to  be clarity in the vision of whatever is going to take English cricket forward with the changes  that are obviously going to happen. When Brendon first took over, we were very clear about what we  wanted to do, and that’s going to be no different for the next role in leadership. It’s going to  be no different for the role of leadership after that. Both captain and coach need to come together  and put their ideas together and believe in what they’re trying to do going forward. And whoever  that may be, then that’s what needs to happen. But again, I’m just going to keep saying I  don’t have to worry about that again. Hi, Ben. Yesterday you spoke about the thoughts  you were having over the last 12 months, and then it was a conversation with Claire,  the two of you being able to talk it through and decide that this was it. Did it need to be  someone who knows you that well to be able to say, look, you should stop, listen to it, because it’s  taking its time? No, not really. I think it was a situation where people just needed to hear me  and I needed to speak. You know, my wife knows me better than anybody else in the world. I spoke to  other people who I’ve got very good relationships with, who I managed to play a lot of cricket  with as well. So, you know, I didn’t just want to limit myself to one person. I wanted to share my  thoughts with quite a few different people and get some different points of view. But at the end of  the day, the decision was always going to be mine. I didn’t really feel like I ever was influenced  by anything other than me. I just felt like even just talking about the whole situation was  just good for me to get my head clear and making sure that I was being completely honest with  myself and taking the right amount of time and measured approach to this whole thing. And I did  that. I got myself through into this game and, as I said before, when I went back for Durham,  I really, really enjoyed it there and I thought I’ll be able to take all of that stuff into this  week. And there were certainly moments this week where I obviously really enjoyed it. But there  are certain moments that you sort of feel like you don’t enjoy as much because of where you are  in terms of representing the whole, the pressure that comes off this level of cricket is something  that, as I said yesterday, maybe I just don’t feel like I have it in me to enjoy those kind of things  anymore. Because cricket for me is something that I love and I always want to love, and I don’t want  to ever feel like I want to get into a place where I have any negative feelings towards it because  I’ve been there before. This sport’s given me so much that I don’t want to find myself back there.  And the moments that I had back at Durham with my boyhood club, it was just all smiles, it was just  all good vibes, it was all happiness. That’s all I want to do because I played this game for fun and  excitement and enjoyment when I was a kid. Just because I’m 35 and I’ve played a lot of cricket  for this country doesn’t mean that should be any different. And for all the games before that,  that’s what I felt. But unfortunately, now I’m at a stage where there are just certain things that  don’t fill me with that same enjoyment anymore. I mean, yeah, I’m not afraid to say that because I  just love the sport too much to have any negative feelings towards it anymore. Are we going to see  you again for Durham this summer or are you going to take a bit of time off? That’s a no. Yeah, I  text Ryan Campbell last night just saying, up the Ds, I’ve got a few days away with the family and  then I’ll let you know what my plans are. And he text me back saying, I’ve probably got a rookie  contract on the table for you if you want it. But yeah, look, my plan was to go back and play  some games for Durham in the Metro Bank anyway, in between these two series. That will probably  change now. But yeah, again, when I said yesterday some of the emotions I was going through, I said  one of them was excitement. I’m excited about the prospect that I get to go back and play  some more games with Durham because, again, I look at it that without Durham and when I was  younger, the progression that I made through into the first team, without them, I wouldn’t be sat  here talking about all this kind of stuff now. So, yeah, it’s a case of going back and having a bit  of fun playing, but also, I guess, repaying some of the stuff that they’ve given to me to allow  me to have played as much as I have for England. Can I just ask, whose idea was it for you to open  last night and what was the thinking behind that? Yeah, it was something that we’d spoken  about sort of as the game progressed, really, when we were seeing that the wicket was starting  to get a little bit trickier to play on. Look, there’s no doubt that the weather obviously  played a big part in that over the first two, two and a half days because of the extreme heat.  So I don’t think it takes rocket science to notice how the scores changed from 320 for none to how  it ended up playing out. The heat made that wicket dry out. There were balls going up, there were  balls going down, there were cracks starting to show. And that’s the exciting thing about this  game, this format, is that the next day is always different to the one you played on, and you know  it’s going to be different the next day as well. So as the game got further and further, it was  obvious that the newer ball and the harder ball, yes, it probably felt like it was the easiest time  to score because there was more attacking field, so there were less fielders to have to hit  through, if that makes sense. But also it was actually the most dangerous time in terms  of taking wickets. So we were like, well, we need to try and capitalise on the best time for  scoring whilst also making it pretty difficult for New Zealand to feel like they could go with their  attacking field in terms of slips and everything around it. So look, two ways where we come off  four down before, it would have been great if we were only two down, but we felt we’d made a  massive dent in such a big total because we were never going to not try and chase that total down  because we’re 1-1. We felt the best way for us to be able to chase that score down was to score  as many runs as possible when the ball was at its hardest, because as the ball got softer, you could  see that the ring fields came into play more. It was harder to force the ball through and the less  amount of runs we had to score on the last day, we thought that was giving ourselves the best  chance to do it. It was unfortunate that we ended up losing four wickets last night, but it  was a complete and utter tactical decision that we made to send the people up the order who  we felt were going to give us the best chance of scoring quick runs. Ben, you talked about that  game you played for Durham. You enjoyed it and the feeling that it gave you about playing cricket.  But then, you know, there are certain things about playing for England that are stopping you from  having that enjoyment. What are those things? Quite a lot. You know, even doing  the extra responsibilities now at 35, I don’t mean this in any negative way whatsoever  for you guys, but just this kind of stuff. You know, I don’t have to worry about speaking to the  media about certain things anymore. I can just go out and play for Durham and play the game and  if I’ve had a good day, if I’ve had a bad day, I can just go home, have a bit of dinner and then  wrap up the next day. I know it sounds silly, but it’s something that if you do go through, it  does take its toll, I guess, and I definitely feel like it has done. There’s a lot of things where  it becomes mentally tiring. Some of the stuff that gets thrown on your shoulders as captain of the  team, but also as a player, the extra scrutiny, the extra expectation from the sport at this  level is something that never really bothered me, it never really fussed me. But as I’ve got closer  to the end of my career, I guess I felt like it has started to take its toll a little bit. And  as I said earlier, I don’t want to feel like I’m having to do things because it’s the right  thing to do for other people. A huge part of this decision is because of what I think is right  for me to still want to be able to play cricket with a smile on my face. And even in the build-up  to the game last week at Lord’s, after six months of being away, I should have been buzzing and  ecstatic and excited about everything that week was to offer. But when I got myself into that,  it sort of wasn’t how I thought it should be. I hope that makes a little bit of sense. I don’t  know if I’ve made that very clear or well enough. But yeah, it does take its toll and there are a  lot of things that go on that people don’t see, you know, back at home, all this kind of stuff.  So I know you said you’ve been thinking about this for a long time and at Lord’s it didn’t feel  right, but then did everything that happened after Lord’s accelerate those feelings? And might  you have been tempted to hang on for a little bit longer if you hadn’t gone through what you’ve  been through in the past couple of weeks? It’s an interesting one because I think if the situation  that unfolded didn’t happen, we’re either going to be here talking about this or not. And it was just  that quite a few things that I was feeling ended up being told to a few more people than I was  expecting to know. And you either would have known or you wouldn’t have known, because I was feeling  like I’ll get myself through to the end of this and we’ll see where we are. And people would have  known or people would have been none the wiser, except my wife. But, you know, just as I say,  because of the circumstance, things just changed. And that was another thing that I sort of had to  deal with over two and a half weeks. But yeah, I don’t know, maybe it has contributed a little  bit, but it’s not the overriding factor as to why I’ve come to this decision. Because one way or  the other, this day was always going to happen and it just happens to be now. Ben, you were always  the champion of Test cricket and obviously now you’re bowing out. What would you say, how  would you sell the game of Test cricket to those that will come after you? How would you  encourage them to tackle it like you have? I guess whenever someone new comes into the  dressing room or into the environment and they are coming in to make their debut or whatever it  is, I guess the one message that I feel like I’ve always said is, don’t feel like you have to change  because you’re now in the dressing room. You’ve got yourself here because of the way that you  play and you’ve been successful at doing that at one level. So go out there and do the exact  same thing that’s got you here in the first place. Just do things your way, do it how you want to do  it. Do what you think is going to give yourself the best opportunity of being successful. And  most importantly, try your hardest to enjoy it, because you need to try and keep hold of  that inner child of playing in the garden with your friends or down the park with your  friends, where everything’s just fun. Now, you throw on top of that expectation, pressure  from playing in front of 25, 30,000 people, millions of people across the world. But if you  break it down and simplify it, it’s just another game of cricket. And that’s how you deal with  those extra things that come with it. You either, as I say, let it eat you up or you just embrace it  all. Because when you’re a kid, you dream of doing that. You dream of playing for England and you  dream of playing international cricket. You dream of walking out in front of these people. And then  if you’re lucky enough to be able to find yourself in that situation, don’t let it feel bigger  than what it is. Because when you’re younger, it’s all you want to do. And then you work so  hard to get there. Try your hardest not to make it bigger than what it is. You’ve said that many  reasons came into why you’re leaving now. Was the Ashes defeat bigger for you than perhaps first  acknowledged at the end of that series? Did that take more out of you than perhaps you wanted it  to? Yeah, maybe. But I think also the six months after that was probably another thing as well.  There was a lot of time physically getting myself ready again for the summer, going through things  that we wanted to feel like we needed to improve as a team, or I wanted to improve as a captain,  as a leader. So I spent a lot of time, as I say, doing things away from the eye of the world,  if that makes sense. And if I look back on it, did I maybe put myself through too much? I could  probably say, yeah, I did. And that’s something that I’ll always maybe be questioning myself.  If I had just taken things a little bit easier, would it have changed things? I don’t know.  But then again, I can flip it around and go, well, that’s what I’ve always done. I’ve always  thrown myself into everything that I’ve done. Is it just meant to be my time? So, yeah, I don’t  know. Australia is always tough, and it was tough, but then obviously it was a tough six months after  that as well. So, yeah, there’s a lot of things. Ben, one of the things you said you were always  going to try to do was to make the dressing-room environment happier and less pressured. Having  been Joe’s friend and vice-captain and seeing what he went through, was there anything you did to try  and make captaining happier and less pressured, yet the burden hang less heavily? Anything  that I did? I think it’s gone in phases, sort of how I wanted to lead the team, to  be honest. To look back at the first summer, there were reasons why we were doing what we were  doing. We then started off like a house on fire, and I’ve said this openly, I had absolutely no  idea how it was going to go. It could have been absolutely horrendous. We could have lost  seven from seven, but we ended up winning six from seven, was it? And everyone’s really  happy, I’m really happy, I’m thinking, jeez, how easy is this? And then you build on that,  and then you start seeing the tough side of the job. And when everything else starts coming  in with that, the scrutiny of being a captain, the scrutiny towards a team when things don’t  go well. So, you know, I’ve always tried to speak in a way which tries to get the players  not thinking about all that kind of stuff. And it is a tough thing to do. And yeah, I guess for  myself, maybe towards the back end of this job, maybe I did put way too much pressure on myself.  But four and a half years doing this job, it is a long time. It has come with a lot of pressure,  something that I will never look back on with any regret because it’s been absolutely awesome  through all the good times, all the bad times, because I’m one of the very few lucky people  to get to do this job. And I’ll always love everything that came with it, through the  good times and all the bad times. But yeah, just always tried to speak in a way that directed  the team’s attention away from maybe what was being said outside. And just on the choreography  of yesterday, you’re pushing yourself through one of these massive spells. You presumably knew when  the bombshell was going to drop. Did you want to be bowling when the news broke? The choreography?  It sounds like you made it sound like a dance routine. I mean, if we had the ability to be  able to script a full day of Test cricket, I would script it that we win every single game.  But it just so happens that I was in the middle of a long spell because of how well the team was  operating. I felt like I was creating a lot of chances whilst also going nowhere. We were taking  wickets at the other end. And then it just so happened that I was bowling when the announcement  came. And not going to lie, I did have a bit of a laugh saying, like, typical, I would have to  take a wicket the next ball. Then, obviously, going out to open the batting, as I explained  before, that was a tactical thing that we’d been speaking about for a few days before. So, yeah,  look, I think we can please try and edge away from saying it was choreographed for that whole day  because we would be absolute geniuses. I mean, we’d have to get New Zealand in on that as well if  that was the case. So we didn’t ask Tom to declare so I could open the batting on my last day. It  just worked out how it worked out and, yeah, that’s it. Sorry to move on. Ben, thanks again  for all the pleasure you’ve given us all through the years and it’s been a privilege to watch  you play. How would you like to be remembered? Oh, just someone who knew what it always meant to  wear an England shirt, did everything that they could to win and just tried the hardest every  single time that they walked onto the field and left everything out there on every single  occasion. I’d like to think I’ve done that for pretty much every game that I wore the shirt, so  hopefully people can all agree with that. That’s what I tried to do. And then everything else  outside of that, wins, losses, whatever it may be, that comes secondary to hard effort and everything  like that to me. So I hope that’s what people can say. Ben, just on the crowd, the reception that  you got when the news did break, was that a moment of personal clarity? I know we’ve talked about the  steps in you had, and maybe did the crowd energise you a little bit more to throw up on the night?  I’m not going to lie, it did. That’s one of the feelings that I’m going to miss as an England  player, is when the crowd gets behind you and gets on your back, because I’ve had quite a few  moments where I’ve felt that, and it does take you from where you feel like you’re at the top of  your adrenaline level and then you find even more. That made me feel like I could just keep going and  going and going and going again. I felt fresh as a daisy after that, even though I bowled quite a  lot of overs in that spell. But I absolutely love playing at Trent Bridge. I’ve got some pretty  good memories anyway. This is where I scored my first first-class hundred against Notts back  in 2010. I won the Ashes here and I’ve seen some pretty special performances from England players  and some players that we played against as well. So I’ve got unbelievable memories here as an  international player and as an England player, as a captain. So yeah, I’ve absolutely loved playing  at this ground. It’s awesome. The atmosphere is always class. So if there’s anything, I feel quite  lucky that this is where I would have walked off the field for my last time as a player because of  all the fond memories I’ve got. Thank you. Thanks all. Sorry, just from me, guys, four and a half  years of doing what I’ve done, I’ve loved every moment of coming and talking to you guys. No, I  do. I understand the responsibility I’ve got as captain to take the good with the smooth, the nice  questions, the tough questions. And, you know, I’ve had up and down days. But I appreciate that  you guys have all got a job to do and there are no hard feelings whatsoever about some of the  pressing questions that you’ve asked me over the years. So I just wish you all the best in  your jobs still. So thanks very much. Cheers.
title: STOKES: “NOT MY PROBLEM ANYMORE!”  Retiring England captain Ben Stokes after NZ defeat
